title: An Inspector Calls: responsibility, class, age and gender
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: modern drama, An Inspector Calls
AO1 and AO3: ideas and the contexts that shaped them

tips.title: One line per theme
tips.body: Responsibility: we are members of one body. Class: girls of that class, and these girls aren't cheap labour. Age: you don't seem to have learnt anything. Gender: the strike and the refused money. Four themes, four lines, all from memory.

tips.title: Two speeches, one test
tips.body: Birling in Act 1 and the Inspector in Act 3 are the poles of the play, and every character is tested between them. Any theme paragraph can start from that contrast, because every theme is a side of the same choice.

tips.title: The theme comes through a character
tips.body: AQA asks how Priestley uses Mrs Birling to explore class, or the Inspector to suggest social change. Plan from the character's moments, name the method, and end on the idea; never start from a definition of the theme.

tips.title: Link two themes in one sentence
tips.body: Mrs Birling refuses responsibility because the girl is of that class. One sentence, two themes, and an argument rather than a list. The top level calls this conceptualised, and it is the quickest way to reach it.

tips.title: Context that explains, not context that fills
tips.body: 1945, the welfare state, the two wars: each is worth a sentence only when it explains a choice Priestley made. A paragraph of history on its own is the AO3 the scheme does not reward.

tips.title: Gerald breaks the pattern
tips.body: Young, honest, and on the side of the parents. Use him whenever a question is about the generations: he shows that the line is drawn by responsibility, and that is an alternative reading the examiners look for.

why.matters: A play with a message is a risk: said flatly, the message is a lecture and the audience stops listening. Priestley's answer was to build his four ideas into one argument and dramatise it as a choice, made in front of the audience by people the audience has come to know. Responsibility is the claim, class is why it is refused, age is who might accept it, and the girl's life is the evidence. The exam asks for the themes through the characters, and pays most for an essay that sees them as one argument rather than four topics. Knowing how the argument is built is what lets a student write that essay.

examples.title: The welfare state the audience was about to build
examples.body: The election of July 1945 returned a government that set out to build a health service and national insurance against sickness and unemployment: help for exactly the people a girl like Eva Smith could not get help from in 1912. Priestley's London audience watched a committee refuse a pregnant girl the year after voting for a state that would not. The play's themes were that year's politics, staged.

examples.title: A story that asks whose fault it was
examples.body: Every serious drama about a death, a disaster or a company collapse ends up asking the play's question: was it one person's fault, or the fault of everyone who shut a door? Inquiries into real disasters, from a building fire to a bank failure, are argued in exactly those terms. Priestley's chain is a model of how shared responsibility is shown rather than asserted.

steps.title: Responsibility: the play's spine
steps.body:
Every other idea in the play hangs from this one. Priestley states the two positions in two speeches and then tests five people between them.

**Birling's position**, Act 1: “A man has to mind his own business and look after himself” (Mr Birling, Act 1). A man answers for himself and his family, and the rest is not his affair. The strike was bad for business, so the ringleader was sacked, and what became of her afterwards is nothing to do with him.

**The Inspector's position**, Act 3: “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” (the Inspector, Act 3). Nobody's actions stop at their own front door. The girl was pushed from one of them to the next, and “each of you helped to kill her” is the verdict on all five.

**The test.** Each character is shown what they did and asked, in effect, which speech they believe. Sheila and Eric accept the second: “I did what I did” (Eric, Act 3). Their parents keep the first: “I did nothing I'm ashamed of” (Mrs Birling, Act 2). Gerald tells the truth and then reaches for the ring. The theme is not stated and left; it is dramatised as a choice, and the audience is left holding the same choice.

rows: Admits it; then wants it undone
props.title: The test of responsibility

visuals.alt: A table of the five characters, what each did to the girl, and whether each accepts responsibility by the end

check.prompt: Which pair of speeches does Priestley set against each other to state the two positions on responsibility?
check.solution: The two speeches are the poles of the play: self-interest in Act 1, shared responsibility in Act 3. Priestley gives each its own act and its own speaker so that the audience can hear one against the other, and everything between them is the test.

markScheme.description: Birling's speech in Act 1 about a man looking after himself, and the Inspector's speech in Act 3 about members of one body

Gerald's account of the summer in Act 2 and Eric's confession about the money in Act 3, which show two young men taking responsibility

steps.title: Class: who counts as a person
steps.body:
In 1912 there was no welfare state. A worker sacked had no unemployment pay; a girl without a family had work, charity or the street. Priestley builds the chain out of exactly those doors, and each one is held by someone who thinks of the girl as a type rather than a person.

**The employer.** To Birling the strikers are a cost. Sheila's answer, “But these girls aren't cheap labour – they're people” (Sheila, Act 1), is the play's plainest statement of the theme.

**The lady on the committee.** Mrs Birling speaks of “girls of that class”, and the phrase is the theme in three words: a class is a thing you can refuse.

**The men at the bar.** Gerald and Eric meet the girl in the Palace bar, where the well-off go to find girls who have nowhere else. What looked like a rescue to Gerald was still a transaction between someone with money and someone without.

**The answer.** The Inspector's “millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths” widens one girl into a class, and the one body speech says what the family's rank is for: nothing, unless it is used for the people below it. The June 2024 mark scheme lists ideas about differences in social class, selfishness and snobbery, and boss and worker in a capitalist society, and every one of them is carried by a moment in the chain.

check.prompt: Why does Sheila's line that the girls are not cheap labour but people matter for the theme of class?
check.solution: The line is the theme in one sentence. Birling sees a cost, Mrs Birling a class, the men at the bar an opportunity; Sheila sees a person. Priestley gives the correction to the character who will go on to accept her own share, so that seeing the girl as a person and taking responsibility for her are shown to be the same thing.

markScheme.description: It names the mistake every door in the chain makes: treating a person as a type, a cost or a case

options: It marks the moment Sheila decides to break off her engagement to Gerald and leave the family
It names the mistake every door in the chain makes: treating a person as a type, a cost or a case
It shows that Sheila is a socialist and has been reading about the strikes in the newspapers her father takes
It proves that Birling paid his workers less than other employers in Brumley and knew it

steps.title: Age: the two generations
steps.body:
The play ends with the family split, and the split runs by age. Mr and Mrs Birling take the news that there was no Inspector as the end of the matter. Sheila and Eric take it as no difference at all. Sheila's verdict on her parents, “you don't seem to have learnt anything” (Sheila, Act 3), is the theme in one line.

**Why age?** Priestley wrote for 1945, and the generation that would build the country after the war was young. The older Birlings are 1912: certain, comfortable and unteachable. The young are the audience's chance. Eric's bitterness, “You're not the kind of father a chap could go to” (Eric, Act 3), is a failure of the older generation as well as of a father.

**Gerald complicates it.** He is young and sides with the old, which tells the audience that the line is really drawn by who accepts responsibility; age is the pattern, not the rule. Use that: it is the kind of alternative reading the top level of the mark scheme asks for.

rows: A case; a class; a nuisance
Real or not, he was right
props.title: Old and young

visuals.alt: A table contrasting the older and younger generations on the girl, the Inspector, the ending and what each stands for in 1945

check.prompt: What does Gerald, young but on the side of the parents, add to the theme of the generations?
check.solution: Gerald breaks the pattern and so shows what the pattern is made of. The play divides people by what they do with the truth, and the young usually do better; Gerald is the exception that makes the rule visible, and a sentence saying so is an alternative reading, which the top level rewards.

markScheme.description: That the real line is drawn by who accepts responsibility, and age is only the pattern along which it usually falls

options: That the young are just as bad as the old, and Priestley has no hope for either generation or for the country they will make between them
That Gerald is older than he looks and should be counted with the parents for that reason
That the real line is drawn by who accepts responsibility, and age is only the pattern along which it usually falls
That the engagement will go ahead after all, because Gerald and the parents agree about everything

steps.title: Gender: what a woman could do in 1912
steps.body:
The girl's life is the play's evidence about women. Her choices were a factory wage, a shop, a bar where men with money looked for company, and a charity run by ladies who decided who deserved help. When each of those failed she had nothing, and the men in the play could walk away from what they did to her.

**Three women, three positions.** Eva Smith has no power at all. Sheila has the power of a customer and uses it once, badly, and learns. Mrs Birling has the power of a committee and uses it to refuse. Priestley puts a woman at each level of the class system and shows what each does with the woman below her.

**The men decide what the women should hear.** The June 2024 mark scheme lists ideas about the impact of stereotypes of female behaviour. Sheila is treated as someone to be kept from unpleasantness and turns out to be the clearest-sighted person in the room, which is Priestley's answer to the stereotype.

rows: None: a wage, a shop, a bar, a charity
Leads a strike; refuses stolen money
props.title: Three women, three positions

visuals.alt: A table of the three women in the play, the power each has in 1912 and what each does with it

check.prompt: How does Priestley use the three women to make a point about class as well as gender?
check.solution: Eva, Sheila and Mrs Birling stand at three levels, and the theme is what each does downward: nothing, a whim, a refusal. Gender and class are shown together because the girl is harmed by women as well as by men, and by the class system that puts them in order.

He shows that all three women are treated identically by the men in the play, whatever their class or their age

steps.title: Building a theme paragraph
steps.body: A theme question still pays twelve marks for methods. The paragraph has to carry an idea, a method and a moment together.

visuals.problem: Write a paragraph on responsibility that would reach the top levels.

steps.text: The idea, in a sentence with Priestley as the subject: Priestley dramatises responsibility as a choice between two speeches.
steps.note: Not *the play is about responsibility*. Say what the writer does with the idea.

steps.text: The first pole, with its line: Birling in Act 1, “A man has to mind his own business and look after himself”.
steps.note: Evidence from memory; the act matters.

steps.text: The second pole, with its line: the Inspector in Act 3, “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other”.
steps.note: The two lines set against each other is the method: contrast.

steps.text: The test, with a moment: Sheila keeps the second position when the others let it go, and says so.
steps.note: A moment from the end of the play; whole text covered.

steps.text: The context that explains: written in 1945 for an audience choosing what kind of country to rebuild.
steps.note: AO3 in one sentence, tied to the choice the play stages.

check.prompt: Which opening sentence for a paragraph on class would the mark scheme place highest?
check.solution: The sentence about the chain of doors says what Priestley does with the theme and points at the method. The sentence calling class a very important theme is a label, the one about the strict class system of 1912 is history without the play, and the one about the middle-class Birlings and the working-class girl is a summary with a cause attached. The scheme wants a conceptualised response, which means an idea about what the writer built.

steps.title: Themes are asked through characters
steps.body:
AQA does not ask *write about responsibility*. In June 2024 the two questions were how Priestley uses the character of Mrs Birling to explore ideas about social class, and how Priestley uses the Inspector to suggest the need for social change. The theme comes through a character, and the answer has to keep both in view.

**So plan from the character's moments.** For Mrs Birling and class: the committee, the name, the phrase about girls of that class, the trap, the relief. For the Inspector and social change: the questioning, the contrast with the family, the speech.

**And keep the theme as the destination.** Each paragraph starts from what the character says or does, names the method, and ends on the idea. The mark scheme's three columns for each question, AO1 details, AO2 methods, AO3 ideas, are the same shape every time.

rows: The committee; the name; the trap; the relief
Selfishness and snobbery; class differences; how society could be organised
The questioning; the contrast; the speech
Boss and worker; class and ordinary lives; caring for one another

steps.title: Which theme does the line carry?
steps.body:
For each line, name the theme it most directly carries, then the second theme it touches. Most lines carry two, which is how the essay links its paragraphs.

1. “girls of that class”
2. “you don't seem to have learnt anything”
3. “But these girls aren't cheap labour – they're people”
4. “You're not the kind of father a chap could go to”
5. “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other”

Then take one line and write the sentence that would follow it in an essay: what Priestley does with it, and for whom.

steps.title: One argument, not four topics
steps.body:
The top level of the mark scheme asks for a conceptualised response: an idea about the whole text, not a set of paragraphs on separate themes. In this play the four themes are one argument seen from four sides.

**Responsibility** is the claim: we are members of one body. **Class** is the reason it is refused: a class is a thing you can decline to see. **Age** is the hope: the young can learn what the old will not. **Gender** is the evidence: the girl's life is what the class system does to the person with least power in it.

**Write the links.** *Mrs Birling refuses responsibility because the girl is of that class; Sheila accepts it because she has seen the girl as a person; the difference between them is the difference between 1912 and what 1945 might become.* One sentence, three themes, and an argument the examiner can follow.

An essay that does this reads as a whole. An essay that takes the themes one at a time reads as a list, however good the paragraphs.

boxes.title: The evidence

visuals.alt: Four boxes showing the four themes as one argument: responsibility the claim, class the refusal, age the hope, gender the evidence

check.prompt: Which sentence links two themes into one argument in the way the top level rewards?
check.solution: The sentence about Mrs Birling refusing because the girl is of that class makes class the reason for the refusal of responsibility, so the two themes become one claim about two characters. The sentences that call class and responsibility two important themes, describe the two women's class and personalities, or assign one theme to each character are the list the top level warns against.

steps.title: Four themes, one argument
steps.body:
Priestley wrote a play with one argument and gave it four faces.

- **Responsibility:** two speeches, Birling's in Act 1 and the Inspector's in Act 3, and five people tested between them; Sheila and Eric accept, the parents refuse, Gerald tells the truth and wants it undone.
- **Class:** four doors shut on a girl because of what she was taken to be, a cost, a servant, an opportunity, a case; Sheila's line that these girls are people is the correction.
- **Age:** the old learn nothing and the young change; Gerald shows the line is really drawn by responsibility.
- **Gender:** three women at three levels of the class system, and what each does with the one below her.
- **In the exam:** themes are asked through characters; plan from the character's moments, name the method, end on the idea, and link the themes into one argument.

Learn one line for each theme and you can open a paragraph on any of them from memory.

questions.solution: A shop, a bar, a charity: there was no welfare state in 1912, and each option is a door held by someone in the play. Priestley builds the chain out of the choices a working girl actually had.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley give the correction that these girls are people to Sheila rather than to the Inspector?
questions.solution: Sheila sees the girl as a person before she knows her own link, and later accepts her share. Priestley makes the two go together in one character: the theme of class and the theme of responsibility are the same thing seen twice.

questions.prompt: What does Eric's complaint that his father is not the kind of father a chap could go to add to the theme of the generations?
questions.solution: The line makes the gap between the generations a cause of harm, not just a difference of opinion. Priestley shows a young man with nowhere to take his trouble, and the older generation is answerable for that too.

questions.solution: The three women are placed in the class system and judged by what they do downward. Gender is not separate from class in the play; the girl is harmed by women as well as men, and by the order that ranks them.

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley make the girl's life, rather than a speech, his main evidence about class?
questions.solution: The chain is the argument made visible: each door is a class judgement, and the audience watches what the judgements add up to. The Inspector's speech names what the chain has already shown.

markScheme.description: Because a life pushed through the doors of the class system shows what the system does, where a speech would only assert it

Because speeches about class were banned on the London stage in 1946
Because Priestley did not trust his audience to follow a speech about politics, and thought a story would be easier for them to understand

questions.prompt: Complete the theme in one word: the older generation learns nothing and the younger generation changes, so the play's hope lies with the ...
questions.solution: The young. Sheila and Eric change; their parents do not; and Priestley wrote for an audience in 1945 whose future would be built by the generation that had fought the war.

It is acceptable only if each paragraph has at least two quotations

questions.prompt: How does Priestley present ideas about responsibility in An Inspector Calls? Write one analytical paragraph that could open the essay, using the two speeches as poles, one character who is tested between them, and a sentence of context that explains why the choice was staged in 1945.
questions.solution: Priestley dramatises responsibility as a choice between two speeches and then tests five people between them. The first is Birling's in Act 1, “A man has to mind his own business and look after himself”, delivered by a man the audience has already heard be wrong about the Titanic and the war, so that the position arrives discredited before the doorbell rings. The second is the Inspector's in Act 3, “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other”, spoken after the chain has been laid out link by link, so that it arrives as a verdict rather than a slogan. Between the two Priestley places Sheila, whose small cruelty at Milwards is the first link admitted with any shame, and who keeps the second position when the others let it go: when her parents relax at the news that there was no Inspector, she tells them that “you don't seem to have learnt anything”. The contrast between the two speeches is the method, and Sheila is the audience's proxy in choosing between them. Priestley wrote the play in 1945, for an audience that had just been through a second war after the first and was about to decide what kind of country to rebuild, and the choice he stages between a man's own business and one body was the choice in front of them.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use the character of Mrs Birling to explore ideas about social class? Write one analytical paragraph that could sit in the middle of an answer to this June 2024 question, linking class to responsibility and using at least two checked quotations.
questions.solution: Priestley makes Mrs Birling the character in whom class and the refusal of responsibility are the same thing. When the pregnant girl comes to her committee she speaks of “girls of that class”, and the phrase is the method: a class is a category, and a category can be refused without anyone having been wronged, which is why she can say “I did nothing I'm ashamed of” and mean it. Priestley then turns her rank against her through the dramatic irony of the trap. She insists that the father of the child should answer for it, “It's his responsibility”, while the audience, and Sheila, already know that the father is Eric, so that her class judgement is heard condemning her own son. The contrast with Sheila completes the point: the daughter who has seen the girl as a person accepts her share, and the mother who has seen only a class cannot. Through her Priestley explores the snobbery and selfishness the mark scheme names, and something beyond them: that the class system is a way of not seeing, and that responsibility begins where the seeing does. For an audience in 1945, about to build a welfare state for exactly the girls Mrs Birling refused, that was the argument the play was written to make.

questions.prompt: The Inspector's line about millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths is used in an essay on class. What is the strongest thing to say about it?
questions.solution: The line is the step from a plot to an argument: the girl is one of millions, and what was done to her was done to them. Saying so connects the method, the widening, to the theme, and to the audience of 1945 who were being asked what they owed those millions.

markScheme.description: That it widens one girl into a class through the commonest name in the country, so the chain becomes an account of how a whole class was treated

questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Priestley presents the young as good and the old as bad.' What is the better reading?
questions.solution: The play does not hand out goodness by age. Eric did the most harm; Gerald is young and refuses the lesson. What Priestley shows is that the capacity to learn runs by generation and the choice to learn runs by character, and an essay that sees both is doing the alternative reading the top level rewards.

examTechnique.body:
**Themes are asked through characters.** June 2024: Mrs Birling and social class; the Inspector and social change. Plan from the character's moments, name the method, end on the idea.

**One line per theme, exact.** There is no extract, and a theme paragraph without a quotation from the right act stays in the middle levels.

**Link the themes.** The top level wants a conceptualised argument about the whole text. One sentence that makes class the reason for refusing responsibility does more than a paragraph on each.

**Context explains a choice.** 1945, the wars and the welfare state earn a sentence each, tied to something Priestley did; on their own they earn almost nothing.

**Alternative readings score.** Gerald, young but with the old, is one; the Inspector's nature left open is another. A sentence acknowledging a second reading is what the Level 5 and 6 descriptors ask for.
examinerErrors: Starting from a definition of the theme rather than from what a character says or does.
Writing four separate paragraphs on four themes with nothing to connect them, which reads as a list.
Giving a paragraph of 1912 or 1945 history that explains no choice in the play.
Treating the young as good and the old as bad, without noticing Gerald or the size of what Eric did.
Asserting that the play is about responsibility without showing the two speeches it sets against each other.
Quoting the one body line inexactly, or attributing a line to the wrong character.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer has an idea about the whole play and uses the themes to make it: responsibility as the claim, class as the refusal, age as the hope, the girl's life as the evidence. It answers the question through the named character's moments across the whole text, names a method for each, and quotes exactly from memory. It sees that the two speeches are the poles and that every character is tested between them, notices that Gerald breaks the generational pattern, and ends its paragraphs on what Priestley wanted a 1945 audience to think, with context that explains rather than decorates.
